summary: Describes common, version-independent engineering details for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP), an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains practical details shared by the IPv4 and IPv6 versions of ILNP. It describes how systems keep identity separate from location and notify peers when a location changes.

questions: how are identifiers and locators encoded in ipv6 and ipv4 packets
what dns record types does ilnp introduce
how do icmp locator updates signal connectivity changes
subtitle: Shared packet, transport, DNS, and deployment details for ILNPv4 and ILNPv6.

tldr.problem: The ILNP architecture needs engineering rules for encoding Identifiers and Locators, keeping transport sessions stable, and advertising changing network locations.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes common implementation details, including Identifier and Locator use, an Identifier-Locator Communication Cache, DNS records, and Locator Update messages.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes ILNP as an Experimental Protocol for examination, implementation, and evaluation. It aims to let end systems use ILNP without changing backbone routers.

facts.label: ILNPv6 Locator
facts.value: Upper 64 bits of the IPv6 address

today: RFC 6741 is an Experimental Protocol from the IRTF. The RFC says it is published for examination, experimental implementation, and evaluation.

sections.title: Common Implementation Rules
sections.content:
RFC 6741 covers engineering considerations shared by ILNPv4 and ILNPv6. It complements the architectural description and leaves full, version-specific engineering specifications to other documents.

ILNP changes end-system protocol behavior while aiming to reuse existing IP packet formats and network infrastructure. Transport protocols must use Identifiers in session state, and the engineering design includes DNS records and ICMP Locator Update messages.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives implementation guidance for the IPv4 and IPv6 forms of ILNP. It focuses on end systems and on how they exchange Identifier and Locator information.

sections.title: Identifiers and Locators in Packets
sections.content:
For ILNPv6, the existing 128-bit IPv6 address space carries a Locator in its upper 64 bits and an Identifier in its lower 64 bits. The Locator has the role of a routing prefix, so IPv6 routers can forward packets without distinguishing ILNPv6 from IPv6.

For ILNPv4, the 32-bit IPv4 address fields carry Locators of at most 30 bits. A 64-bit Identifier is carried in an IPv4 option. ILNPv4 requires related ARP changes at the edge, while backbone routers use the address field for forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: ILNPv6 places the Locator and Identifier in different parts of the existing IPv6 address. ILNPv4 uses the IPv4 address for the Locator and an option for the Identifier.

sections.title: Transport State and Checksums
sections.content:
TCP and UDP normally use IP addresses as part of their transport state. ILNP implementations instead use the local and remote Identifiers with the transport ports. The Identifier remains the stable part of that state when a Locator changes.

TCP and UDP pseudo-header checksums include the Identifier values and exclude Locator values. The RFC describes zeroing Locator fields for these calculations. ICMP checksums continue to follow the existing IPv4 or IPv6 calculation for the corresponding ILNP version.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP and UDP keep the node Identifiers in their session state. Their checksums also use Identifiers, so changing a Locator does not change those values.

sections.title: The Cache, DNS, and Locator Changes
sections.content:
The Identifier-Locator Communication Cache (ILCC) keeps the local node's valid Identifiers and Locators, plus information about current or recent correspondents. A correspondent's DNS record Time to Live can inform how long cached Locator information remains valid. Expired Locator data can be retained for an active session while the system waits for an update.

When a node's Locator set changes, it sends an ICMP Locator Update to active correspondents. A node expecting new incoming sessions normally updates its DNS Locator records using Secure Dynamic DNS Update. DNS records named by this RFC's document set include NID, L32, L64, and LP.
sections.plainLanguage: The cache stores the Identifiers and Locators needed to communicate. When a Locator changes, the node tells current correspondents and can update DNS for new connections.

sections.title: Compatibility and Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
ILNPv6 uses the existing IPv6 packet format, and routers need no changes to forward its packets. ILNPv4 also uses the existing IPv4 address fields for routing, but needs an ARP enhancement for ILNP-capable nodes and their first-hop network equipment.

During transition, DNS can contain both ILNP-specific records and ordinary A or AAAA records. An ILNP-capable node can use ILNP records when available and use classic IP when the peer does not advertise ILNP support.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing routers can forward ILNP packets using their IPv4 or IPv6 fields. A node can use ordinary IP records when its peer does not provide ILNP records.
